title: Polynomial-time mixed equilibria in coordination polymatrix games
area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm that, for every finite rational coordination-only polymatrix game, outputs an exact mixed Nash equilibrium in time polynomial in the complete binary input length?
why: Locate the tractability boundary for exact mixed equilibrium when every pairwise interaction has common payoffs, distinguishing the complexity of network coordination from general games and from pure local-search equilibria.
status_note: The exact coordination-only tractability question is open in the checked primary sources. A bounded later-work search on 14 September 2026 found no matching resolution. Pure-equilibrium hardness and the 2025 two-team result concern different tasks; they are not treated as a refutation or an unconditional lower bound for this proposition.

progress.text: Cai–Daskalakis establish pure-equilibrium PLS-completeness and mixed-equilibrium membership in PLS and PPAD, leaving polynomial-time mixed-equilibrium tractability open.
Savani poses the coordination-only mixed-equilibrium complexity question in the Dagstuhl report.
The two-team hardness result allows zero-sum interactions between teams and hence does not settle this coordination-only restriction.

sentences: Each player uses one action across several pairwise interactions in a graph.
The two endpoints of each edge receive equal payoffs from that interaction.
The target is a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm returning any exact mixed Nash equilibrium.
Pure equilibria are permitted outputs, but an algorithm may also use genuinely mixed profiles.
Known pure-equilibrium and adversarial two-team hardness results do not settle this coordination-only mixed search task.

definitions: An instance is a finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), with \(V=\{1,\ldots,r\}\), and for each player \(i\) a nonempty explicitly enumerated action set \(A_i=\{1,\ldots,k_i\}\). Each edge \(\{i,j\}\), with \(i<j\), carries an explicitly listed matrix \(M_{ij}\in\mathbb Q^{k_i\times k_j}\). If its endpoints choose \(a\in A_i\) and \(b\in A_j\), both receive the same edge payoff \(M_{ij}(a,b)\). Set \(M_{ji}(b,a)=M_{ij}(a,b)\) for reverse orientation. Each player selects one action for all its incident edges and receives the sum of those edge payoffs; nonedges contribute zero. A mixed profile \(p=(p_i)_{i\in V}\) uses independent probability vectors \(p_i\) on \(A_i\). For a pure deviation \(a\in A_i\), write \[v_i(a,p_{-i})=\sum_{j:\{i,j\}\in E}\sum_{b\in A_j}p_j(b)M_{ij}(a,b),\qquad u_i(p)=\sum_{a\in A_i}p_i(a)v_i(a,p_{-i}).\] It is an exact Nash equilibrium when \(v_i(a,p_{-i})\le u_i(p)\) for every player \(i\) and every action \(a\). The required output explicitly lists nonnegative rational probabilities summing to one for each player. A pure profile is allowed as a degenerate mixed profile; neither full support nor a genuinely randomizing player is required. Vertices, edges and all actions are listed, and each payoff is encoded by a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator with delimiters. Thus the input length \(N\) includes the action lists, graph and every payoff bit; no succinct payoff circuit is allowed. Use a uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine with a fixed finite program, no advice or oracles, and a bound \(C(N+1)^d\) on all valid inputs for constants \(C,d\) independent of the instance. Charge every bit operation and output bit. The target is exact equilibrium, with no approximation parameter or promise on payoff magnitudes, graph degree or action counts.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the existence of the stated uniform polynomial-time algorithm, including termination, the full bit bound and exact equilibrium correctness, or of its logical negation. A hardness reduction under an unproved separation establishes only a conditional conclusion. A polynomial bound in numerical payoff magnitudes, a fixed graph or action-count special case, or an approximate-equilibrium algorithm without an exact guarantee does not meet the target.

context_blocks.text: Coordination is imposed locally: the two endpoints agree on the payoff of their shared interaction. A player with several neighbors must nevertheless choose one action that participates in all those interactions. Equal payoffs on each edge therefore do not mean that every player has the same total payoff on every full profile.

For example, on a three-vertex path, the middle player receives the sum from both edges, while each endpoint receives only its single edge payoff. The middle player can face conflicting preferences from its two interactions even though each separate interaction gives identical rewards to its two participants.

The 2014 Dagstuhl report attributes the network-coordination question to Rahul Savani and explicitly imposes equality in each edge’s payoff pair. The present card makes polynomial-time tractability the binary target of that broader complexity question; Cai and Daskalakis already explicitly ask whether this search problem is in P.

Cai and Daskalakis show that finding a pure equilibrium is complete for polynomial local search, abbreviated PLS, while finding any mixed equilibrium belongs to both PLS and the parity-based total-search class PPAD. Permitting mixed output changes the search task even though pure equilibria exist: hardness of finding a pure equilibrium alone does not classify the task that may return any mixed one.

The same primary source records that rational polymatrix games have mixed equilibria with rational probabilities and polynomial description length. Exact output is consequently meaningful in the bit model and is not obstructed by a need to print arbitrary irrational numbers.

Hollender, Maystre and Nagarajan prove hardness for two-team polymatrix games with coordination inside teams and zero-sum interactions between teams. Their result allows adversarial edges absent from this card, and therefore does not classify coordination-only games. Likewise, an equilibrium constrained to be symmetric is a different output requirement.

The question tests whether permitting players to randomize makes arbitrary networks of local common-interest interactions computationally tractable. The input restriction and the freedom to return any equilibrium both matter; neither general-game hardness nor the ease of a single two-player coordination game settles this network case.
